hypothesis: The unidentified aqueous-phase metabolite feature with molecular formula C13H26N5O12S is increased/characteristic in 12-month-old infants fed a meat-based complementary diet relative to a dairy-based complementary diet.
rationale: Searches for the exact molecular formula ("C13H26N5O12S") returned no compound record, no database entry, and no publication reporting this formula in any biological matrix - only unrelated set-index pages for other molecular formulas. Because the feature has no chemical name/identity (annotation is a bare formula from untargeted MS), no literature can directly address it, and there is therefore no study on this feature + meat-vs-dairy complementary feeding combination. What searches did retrieve is contextual literature on the same type of exposure: the Colorado randomized meat- vs. dairy-based complementary feeding trial in formula-fed U.S. infants (5-12 months), which reports diet-group differences in serum metabolomics (notably amino acid/BCAA-related shifts) and, in the accompanying network-representation-learning analysis of paired fecal metagenomes and metabolomes, enrichment of microbial genes for amino acid, nucleic acid and carbohydrate metabolism in the meat group. That makes it plausible in a purely generic sense that a nitrogen- and sulfur-containing (i.e. amino-acid/nucleotide-derived) polar metabolite could track with higher meat protein intake, since meat is richer in sulfur amino acids (methionine, cysteine, taurine) and in purine/nucleotide substrates than dairy. This is pathway-level, theoretical reasoning only, with no feature-specific data, which maps to a confidence score of 1 rather than 2. An additional technical caution: for a neutral, even-electron molecule the formula C13H26N5O12S gives a half-integer ring-plus-double-bond equivalent (13 - 26/2 + 5/2 + 1 = 3.5), violating the nitrogen rule, so the formula as given is most consistent with an adduct/ion form or an ambiguous formula assignment - reinforcing that no confident literature match is possible.

evidence.title: Different Blood Metabolomics Profiles in Infants Consuming a Meat- or Dairy-Based Complementary Diet
evidence.study_population: Formula-fed U.S. infants in a randomized controlled complementary-feeding trial, meat vs. dairy protein from 5 to 12 months of age (serum targeted and untargeted metabolomics; ~151 annotated metabolites)
evidence.relevance: Indirect/contextual only: establishes that a meat- vs. dairy-based complementary diet produces measurable metabolomic differences (largely amino-acid related) in infants at the 5-12 month window, but this study reports named metabolites and does not report any feature with formula C13H26N5O12S, so it does not support the hypothesis for this specific feature.

evidence.title: Network-based representation learning reveals the impact of age and diet on the gut microbial and metabolomic environment of U.S. infants in a randomized controlled feeding trial
evidence.study_population: U.S. formula-fed infants, 5-12 months, randomized meat- vs. dairy-based complementary feeding; paired fecal metagenomics and metabolomics
evidence.relevance: Indirect/pathway-level: reports that the meat diet group was enriched for microbial genes in amino acid, nucleic acid and carbohydrate metabolism, giving generic plausibility that N/S-containing amino-acid- or nucleotide-derived polar metabolites could be characteristic of the meat group; no specific unannotated feature with this formula is named as meat-associated in the abstract/text retrieved.

evidence.title: Different gut microbiota in U.S. formula-fed infants consuming a meat vs. dairy-based complementary foods: A randomized controlled trial
evidence.study_population: Full-term, formula-fed U.S. infants randomized to meat- vs. dairy-based complementary foods, 5-12 months
evidence.relevance: Contextual background on the exposure of interest (meat vs. dairy complementary protein at the 12-month timepoint) and its gut microbiota effects; contains no metabolite-level information on this feature.

caveats: The feature is an unannotated untargeted-MS formula with no name, InChIKey, HMDB/KEGG/PubChem ID, or retention-time/MS2 identity, so literature searching cannot be specific; any formula-only match would also be ambiguous across many isomers. The formula additionally yields a half-integer RDBE (3.5), i.e. it violates the nitrogen rule for a neutral even-electron molecule, suggesting it may represent an adduct/ion species or an uncertain formula assignment. Structural confirmation (MS2 spectra, library or in-silico matching) is required before any literature-based directional claim about meat vs. dairy complementary feeding can be evaluated; the score of 1 reflects generic pathway plausibility only, not feature-specific support.
